newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Former Sri Lanka rebel group tries luck with ballot.
newsitem.headline: Former Sri Lanka rebel group tries luck with ballot.

text.p: A former leftwing rebel group which rocked Sri Lanka with two abortive insurgencies takes another shot at mainstream politics in Friday's local government poll, officials and analysts said on Tuesday.

"We want to build an alternative political force to the two capitalist parties which have ruled the country for the past 49 years since independence," said Wimal Weerawansa of the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP or People's Liberation Front).
The party, which last fought an election in 1982, will use the poll as a springboard for the next general election in 2001, Weerawansa, the JVP's propaganda secretary, told Reuters.
Thousands of JVP members were killed in a brutal government crackdown on a rebellion by the mainly youth-based group in 1988-90.
Human rights groups said up to 60,000 people died or disappeared in the violence.

The party emerged from the underground in 1994 and managed to get a single lawmaker elected to parliament in that year's general election, won by the People's Alliance coalition of President Chandrika Kumaratunga.
The JVP first shot to prominence in an ill-planned uprising in 1971 that was crushed with several hundred deaths.
Political analyst Dayan Jayatilleka said the JVP's participation in Friday's poll was a good sign that indicated they were giving electoral politics another chance.

"If they do get a decent representation, they will be more tempted to work the system, which is a good thing for the system and for themselves," Jayatilleka, editor of the independent Lanka Guardian magazine, told Reuters.
"The JVP must realise democratic politics is a hard, boring game and must not allow itself to be provoked by an arrogant government into picking up the gun again," he said.
"If so, it could only mean once again, for the third time, the decimation of its ranks," he added.
The JVP's Weerawansa said the party was compelled to resort to violence during the two abortive insurgencies because they were forced underground by a government ban.
"If the PA or any other regime tries to block us again, we feel we can defeat such attempts democratically," he said.
Jayatilleka said the government should be careful not to provoke the JVP and drive them underground as happened during the two previous uprisings.

"The government must realise that if they use violence against the JVP, it is likely to bite back," he said. "Also, the democratic opposition must bear in mind that it is usually when it is weak that space opens up on their left flank for organisations like the JVP."
Rising unemployment among the youth, which the government had not been able to resolve, could feed the JVP's ranks and fuel its characteristic political impatience, he warned.
The JVP might re-think its parliamentary option if it fails to win a sizeable representation at the poll, he also said.
The JVP is fielding 3,000 candidates and contesting 192 of the 238 councils up for grabs at Friday's poll.

Nearly 20,000 candidates from 12 political parties and 132 independent groups are contesting throughout the Indian Ocean island except in the north and east, where Tamil Tiger separatist rebels are fighting for an independent homeland.
